content: Becker's nevus was first described in 1948 by the American dermatologist Samuel William Becker. This skin condition primarily affects males and typically manifests as irregular pigmentation, known as melanosis or hyperpigmentation, on the torso or upper arm. However, other areas of the body can also be involved. Over time, the lesion tends to enlarge in an irregular pattern, becoming thickened and often developing excessive hair growth, a condition referred to as hypertrichosis. This disorder is also known by several other names, including Becker nevus, Becker's pigmented hairy nevus, Becker melanosis, and pigmented hairy epidermal nevus. The medical understanding of Becker's nevus is limited, likely due to its relatively recent identification, its low prevalence, and the fact that its effects are primarily aesthetic rather than functional. The exact pathophysiology of this condition remains unclear. While it is generally considered an acquired condition rather than a congenital one, there has been at least one documented case suggesting a possible genetic association. This case involved a 16-month-old boy with a hyperpigmented lesion on his right shoulder, whose father had a similar lesion in the same location. The most comprehensive study to date, conducted in 1981, surveyed nearly 20,000 young French men. This study identified 100 cases of Becker's nevus, indicating a prevalence of 0.52%. The lesions appeared before the age of 10 in half of the cases, while the other half developed between the ages of 10 and 20. Contrary to prior beliefs, the study also found that only 32% of lesions occurred above the nipples, challenging the assumption that the upper chest and shoulder were the most common sites. In 75% of cases, the pigmentation was light brown, and the average size of the lesion was approximately 125 cm² (19 in²). In terms of malignancy, a 1991 report documented nine cases of patients who had both Becker's nevus and malignant melanoma. Of these nine melanomas, five were located in the same body region as the Becker's nevus, with only one melanoma occurring within the nevus itself. This was the first documented co-occurrence of the two conditions, and there is currently no evidence to suggest that Becker's nevi have a higher risk of malignancy compared to normal skin. Nevertheless, as with any abnormal skin lesion, it is important to monitor the nevus regularly and report any sudden changes in appearance to a healthcare professional. Diagnosis of Becker's nevus is primarily based on physical examination. The lesion is typically identified by its characteristic appearance, which includes irregular pigmentation and, in many cases, excessive hair growth. Treatment for Becker's nevus is generally not required unless the patient seeks intervention for cosmetic reasons. Unwanted hair can be managed through shaving or trimming, while laser hair removal may provide a more long-lasting solution. Various laser treatments may also be used to reduce or eliminate hyperpigmentation, although the outcomes of such treatments can be highly variable.
